Original message:
********************************************************************
Splus users,
        I'm trying to draw a normal density plot with the shaded area in the
tails indicating 5% (one tail) , or 2.5% (2 tails) (I'm preparing a slide
presentation in PowerPoint for students to show the rejection region in
hypothesis testing)
What I did so far is creating a random sample of a large size from a normal
distribution, and then using some combination of plot(density()), and hist()
functions. I used split.screen(), and screen() to overlay them.
Nothing did the trick so far.
I checked the s-news archives on that, but couldn't find exactly what I
wanted.

Thanx in advance for the help,
Jarek

P.S. I'm using Splus 4.5 for Windows NT.

********************************************************************

Summary of responses:
********************************************************************
Niels Waller, Ph.D.

With a little fiddling, this function should do the trick.     It is called
as follws:

AreaUnderCurve.prg(zvalue)

> AreaUnderCurve.prg
function(z)
{
 z1 <- seq(-3, 3, 0.01)
 height.of.curve <- dnorm(z1)
 AreaBelow <- round(pnorm(z), 3)
 AreaAbove <- 1 - AreaBelow
 plot(z1, height.of.curve, type = "l", xlab = "Z", ylab = "Density of Normal
Curve", main = paste("z = ", as.character(z)))
 text(-2, 0.33, paste("Area below  z = ", 100 * AreaBelow, "%"))
 text(2, 0.33, paste("Area above  z = ", 100 * AreaAbove, "%"))
 z2 <- seq(-3, 3, 0.05)
 height2 <- dnorm(z2)
 len <- length(z2[z2 < z])
 segments(z2[z2 < z], rep(0, len), z2[z2 < z], height2[z2 < z])
}

********************************************************************
Peter Perkins:

why not use lines() to cross hatch the region?  for the right-hand end
of the lines, pick equally spaced points on the x-axis, and get the
y-coord from dnorm(x).  for the left-hand end, use slope-intercept of a
45 degree line to project to the x-axis, or to a vertical line at the
cutoff point.

******************************************************************** 
Z. Todd Taylor

The way I usually do overlaid plots of that sort is like:

   plot(density(), ...)
   par(new=T)
   hist(...)

The par(new=T) lies to S about the state of the graphics
device---it declares that the page is "new" even though it has
already been drawn on.  Then, when the hist() command is run, S
won't advance the page but will draw on top of the existing
graphcis.

Of course, you'll have to ensure that both plots use the same
axis extents (xlim, ylim) and don't draw the axes at all on
one of them.  e.g.,

   x.lim <- c(0,1); y.lim <- c(0,1)  # whatever...
   plot(density(), xlim=x.lim, ylim=y.lim, ...)
   par(new=T)
   hist(..., xlim=x.lim, ylim=y.lim, axes=F, ...)

Hope that helps.

--Todd

********************************************************************
Don MacQueen:

To point you in the right direction (but not a full solution), try
  hist(  ,prob=T)     ## the prob argument to hist()
  lines(density())    ## to add the density to the histogram
-Don

********************************************************************
Mark Smith

Try this script.  Pretty straightforward to generalize into a function with
mean, sd, color, limits, etc.

x<-seq(-4, 4, .01)      # Overkill sequence from very low to very high.
y<-dnorm(x, 0, 1)               # N(0,1) density
plot(x,y, type="l")             # line plot
xlow<-x[x<=-1.96]       # lower alpha/2 point
xlow<-c(xlow, xlow[length(xlow)], xlow[1])              # Lower tail, with
the highest (-1.96) and lowest (-4) point.
xlow<-c(xlow, NA, -xlow)                # Add the upper tail, separated by
an NA
ylow<-c(y[x<=-1.96],0,0)                # N(0,1) density in those two
regions.
ylow<-c(ylow, NA, ylow)
polygon(xlow,ylow,density=-1, col=16)           # density=-1 is full fill.
col=16 is grey for me.

 <<...>> 
********************************************************************
George Tomlinson

Try this:

z<-seq(-3,3,len=200)
crit <- qnorm(c(0.025,0.975))
plot(z,dnorm(z),type="l")
tail.x.values <- z[z>crit[2]]
polygon(c(tail.x.values, rev(tail.x.values)),
c(dnorm(tail.x.values), rep(0,length(tail.x.values))))

tail.x.values <- z[z<crit[1]]
polygon(c(tail.x.values, rev(tail.x.values)),
c(dnorm(tail.x.values), rep(0,length(tail.x.values))))

********************************************************************
Scott Chasalow:

Hi,

You might find two functions I include at the bottom of this email useful.
The first, draw.norm(), I've been using now and then for years.  Its not
very
pretty but it does the job: draw a set of normal densities in a single plot.
The second, shade.norm(), I just came up with in response to the challenge
represented by your email.  With arguments lower.prob and upper.prob you can
specify a single region to shade in each of the densities.  This uses the
type = 'h' option to plotting functions, which yields high-density lines
(essentially, very fine-scale histograms), to do the shading.

The main drawback of this approach is that it may yield very large graphics
files. If this is a problem, you could try reducing the line density; I
chose
10,000 lines to make the shading appear solid, but many fewer probably would
do the trick.

Also, it is the user's responsibility to make sure the mean, sd, and weight
arguments to draw.norm() and shade.norm() agree.  Otherwise you probably
will
get nonsense.

Some examples:

draw.norm()
shade.norm(lower=0.95)

draw.norm()
shade.norm(lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
shade.norm(lower=0.975, upper=0.999)

draw.norm(0:1)
shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.975, upper=0.999)

Good luck,
Scott

=== CUT=============================================

"draw.norm"<-
function(mean = 0, sd = 1, weight = 1, plot = T, tit = T, plotfun =
"matplot",
     type = "l", lty = 1:5, col = 1:6, xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)", ...)
{
# Date written: ?     Last revised:  6 May 1993
     n <- max(length(mean), length(sd))
     mean <- rep(mean, length = n)
     sd <- rep(sd, length = n)
     weight <- rep(weight, length = n)
     x <- NULL
     y <- NULL
     for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
          x <- cbind(x, as.matrix(qnorm(seq(0.001, 0.999, length = 1000),
mean[
               i], sd[i])))
          y <- cbind(y, as.matrix(dnorm(x[, i], mean[i], sd[i])))
     }
     y <- y %*% diag(weight)
     if(plot) {
          eval(parse(text = plotfun))(x, y, type = type, xlab = xlab, ylab =

               ylab, lty = lty, col = col, ...)
          if(tit)
               title(paste("Normal density:\nmean =", deparse(mean), ", sd
=",
                    deparse(sd)))
          invisible(return(NULL))
     }
     return(list(xmat = x, ymat = y))
}
"shade.norm"<-
function(mean = 0, sd = 1, weight = 1, lower.prob = 0.95, upper.prob =
0.999,
     plot = T, plotfun = "matlines", type = "h", lty = 1:5, col = 1:6, ...)
{
# DATE WRITTEN:  14 May 1999             LAST REVISED:  14 May 1999
# AUTHOR:  Scott Chasalow (Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com)
#
# DESCRIPTION:
#       Shade a specified area under the curve of one or more normal
densities.
#
# SEE ALSO:
#       draw.norm, draw.normmix
#
# EXAMPLES:
#
#       draw.norm()
#       shade.norm(lower=0.95)
# 
#       draw.norm()
#       shade.norm(lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
#       shade.norm(lower=0.975, upper=0.999)
# 
#       draw.norm(0:1)
#       shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
#       shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.975, upper=0.999)
#
     n <- max(length(mean), length(sd))
     mean <- rep(mean, length = n)
     sd <- rep(sd, length = n)
     weight <- rep(weight, length = n)
     x <- NULL
     y <- NULL
     for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
          x <- cbind(x, as.matrix(qnorm(seq(lower.prob, upper.prob, length =

               10000), mean[i], sd[i])))
          y <- cbind(y, as.matrix(dnorm(x[, i], mean[i], sd[i])))
     }
     y <- y %*% diag(weight)
     if(plot) {
          eval(parse(text = plotfun))(x, y, type = type, lty = lty, col =
col,
               ...)
          invisible(return(NULL))
     }
     return(list(xmat = x, ymat = y))
}

=====  END CUT
================================================================
********************************************************************

messages.subject: RE: [S] Default settings for trellis
messages.body_plain:
I also wanted a good solution for this, so I took a fresh look at it
(under win9x).

As Bert was saying there are quite a number of data sets
'trellis.settings.*' that can be attached as an attribute to the .Device
object.  However, they are all attached as 'trellis.settings' on the
currently active device.  More importantly they can be changed with
trellis.par.set().

Note, before I go on, that there is a bug in 'render.trellis' that does
not allow, is seems, any list to the argument 'par.strip.text' of
strip.default(), such as the default 'trellis.par.get("add.text")' to ever
be used. [There is a help page for strip.default()]

Looking in render.trellis():

function(..., par.strip.text = list(), ..., strip =strip.default,...)

...................
strip(k, unlist(index[n,  ]), gnames, factor = if(v) NULL else
  glist[[k]]$levels, shingle = if(v) attr(glist, "endpts")[[k]] else NULL,
  par.strip.text = par.strip.text)
.............

Now 'par.strip.text' is an argument to render.trellis() with a default of
'list()'.  So either the default will be used or whatever the user gives
for 'par.strip.text' in a trellis call [such as to xyplot()].

Given this bug, I did the following:  

In render.trellis(), changed the default 'list()' of 'par.strip.text' to

        'trellis.par.get("add.strip.text")'  

'add.strip.text' is new which I create in:

trellis.device.bw <- function(..., label.list = list(cex = 1.2, col = 1,
      font = 1), strip.list = list(cex = 1, col = 1, font = 1))
{
        trellis.device(..., color = F)
        trellis.par.set("strip.background", list(col = rep(0, 7)))
        trellis.par.set("strip.shingle", list(col = rep(0, 6)))
        "Use add.text only for xlab and ylab."
        trellis.par.set("add.text", label.list)
        "Make a new trellis setting for strip text."
        trellis.settings$add.strip.text <- strip.list
        assign("trellis.settings", trellis.settings, frame = 0)
        invisible()

Using trellis.settings in this way works, since from the help on
trellis.settings:

"If there is no trellis.settings attribute on .Device then the functions
will use the values in the trellis.settings data set in the Trellis
library."

(Of course, the functions find my trellis.settings in frame zero first.)

Example:

(Note, the gray from col=3 is probably not what one would want.)

trellis.device.bw(label.list = list(cex = 2, col = 1, font = 1),
        strip.list = list(cex = 0.6, col = 3, font = 1))

states <- data.frame(state.x77,
                     state.name = dimnames(state.x77)[[1]],
                     state.region = state.region)
xyplot(Murder ~ Population | state.region, data = states,
       groups = as.character(state.name),
       panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups) 
       text(x, y, groups[subscripts]))

-------------

This also helps to get full control for color too:

trellis.device.color <- function(..., label.list = list(cex = 1.2, 
  col = 1, font = 1), strip.list = list(cex = 1, col = 1, font = 1))
{
        trellis.device(..., color = T)
        "Use add.text only for xlab and ylab."
        trellis.par.set("add.text", label.list)
        "Make a new trellis setting for strip text."
        trellis.settings$add.strip.text <- strip.list
        assign("trellis.settings", trellis.settings, frame = 0)
        invisible()
}

--

messages.body_plain:
>
> 
> I'm running a simulation in S-PLUS in which a simple GLM is fitted (the
> actual function I'm running is long but the key line is:)

> A new value for ti is generated in each iteration. The true parameter values

> options start and the function glm.control to speed up my calculations?
> 
> I tried start=c(1,0) in the function call but that doesn't work. Thank you
> in 
> advance for your help,
> 

If you run many simulations with the same design matrix, it is convenient 
to call directly  glm.fit(X, Y, <other.parameters>)
which is the workhorse of glm(); from its help page:

DETAILS:
       This function is useful for simulations or  bootstrapping,
       where  you  use  the  same data frame over and over again.
       Using glm.fit for bootstrapping saves a  large  amount  of
       computational  time,  since  it  only fits a glm model and
       does not create the model matrix.  Thus, no formula  needs
       to  be  specified as an argument.  The glm.fit function is
       called internally by glm to do the actual model fitting.

regards

Hi!

   I have just developed a program to calculate
"Hat matrix" for polynomial equation fitting as below:

function()
{
        nd <- 31
        xx <- seq(from = 1, by = 1, length = nd)
        ndim <- 4
        xm <- rep(1, length = nd)
        for(i in 1:ndim) {
                xm <- cbind(xm, xx^i)
        }
        print(xm)
        hatmat <- xm %*% solve(t(xm) %*% xm) %*% t(xm)  #
}

equation. When the value of "ndim" is 1, 2, or 3, this program works

> From: TAKEZAWA Kunio <takezawa at affrc.go.jp>
> 
>    I have just developed a program to calculate
> "Hat matrix" for polynomial equation fitting as below:
> 
> function()
> {
>       nd <- 31
>       xx <- seq(from = 1, by = 1, length = nd)
>       ndim <- 4
>       xm <- rep(1, length = nd)
>       for(i in 1:ndim) {
>               xm <- cbind(xm, xx^i)
>       }
>       print(xm)
>       hatmat <- xm %*% solve(t(xm) %*% xm) %*% t(xm)  #
> }
> 
> The predictors are equi-spaced and the number of data ("nd")
> is 31. The object "ndim" is the degree of the polynomial
> equation. When the value of "ndim" is 1, 2, or 3, this program works
> well. But when I substitute 4 to "ndim", the error below
> comes out:
> Error in solve.qr(a): apparently singular matrix
> 
> I think that the calculation of Hat matrix for 
> 4-degree polynomial is somewhat ill-conditioned but
> it is not impossible if double precision values are
> used.  I am just wondering if the criterion for judging
> whether a matrix is "singular matrix" or not is too severe.

Unlikely.  using kappa (careful: it needs to be applied to qr(a)) or
svd will tell you the condition number of the matrix. This depends
on the scaling of the points, so at least centre and scale your points 
before you start. In your example the condition number is 4.7e12, so
I am not surprised this is considered singular.

However, this is not the right way to calculate the hat matrix: the
textbook formulae rarely are computationally sound. I do not need to
tell you a better way, as lm.influence will show you (using the qr
decomposition).

--

Announcement: New Book on Multivariate Permutation Testing

Pesarin F. (1999) Permutation testing of multidimensional hypotheses by
nonparametric combination of dependent tests.
CLEUP University Publisher, Padova, 343 pages.

This book contains a formal development of the conditioning approach
underlying
permutation testing.
Furthermore, the methodology of nonparametric combination of dependent
permutation tests is widely analyzed in order to obtain simple solutions to
many rather complex multivariate problems. Among these: restricted
alternatives, mixed data, MANOVA for categorical and quantitative variables,
isotonic inference, complete permutation analysis of Two Way ANOVA,
permutation analysis of missing data, the permutation univariate and
multivariate Behrens-Fisher problem, goodness-of-fit for ordered categorical
data, multidimensional testing problems with repeated measurements, MANOVA
with missing data (Missing Completely at Random, MAR data, and not-MAR
data), etc.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Use of latin characters !
messages.body_plain:
From: Ernesto Jardim
> The problem is that when using the "read.table" function to import the
> data the names are imported beteween "" with slashes (\" name \") and
> the special characters are converted in numbers (ç = \347).

The problem with the cedilla and similar characters is not with the way
the data are read in, but with the way they are printed.  Every character
is represented by numbers in the computer but they are not all printed
that way.  By default print() and similar functions will represent
non-standard ASCII characters (e.g.  the ISO Latin extensions that you
are using) using escape sequences for octal coding.  Hence ç = \347.
I'm sure this seems odd to you in an environment where these characters
are part of the standard character set of your language, but not so at
Bell Labs. :-)

Also, some characters are printed out as escape sequences, e.g. \n
for a newline, \t for a tab.  The double quote is one of these, to
distinguish between double quote to delimit the string and double
quote as a character in the string.

If you use cat(), every character goes out as a single character rather
than an escape, e.g. 

> X_"ssdfa\"\347\"as\tdfa\n"
> print(X)
[1] "ssdfa\"\347\"as\tdfa\n"
> cat(X)
ssdfa"ç"as      dfa
> 

If you use write.table() to write out the contents, you also get the
original characters back.

messages.body_plain:
I don't believe this has been asked frequently, if at all.  That seems
to be a very reasonable approach.

This does relate to two projects we - John Chambers and I are
currently "completing".  Since John is currently away, I'll take the
liberty of speaking for him with the usual disclaimers....

John has a general .Java() equivalent of the .C() which allows
on to invoke methods of an object or class with S-level arguments.
It also allows Java code to call functions/methods in S.
This works by embedding the Java Virtual Machine within
the S process.

A different approach uses CORBA to allow method invocation in a
(possibly remote) application to be invoked as a pseudo-S
function. This is the .Corba() function and allows structured
high-level interprocess and inter-machine communication. Likewise, one
can create S-level CORBA servers from user-level objects and functions
and these can be exploited by arbitrary code connecting to them via
CORBA.

The .Java relies on S4/Splus5 and JDK2.  The CORBA mechanism is almost
S3 compatible and will support not only S, but R, Octave and most
likely Xlisp and Matlab. Both will be released as part of the Omegahat
project, most likely in about two months.
Keep an eye on
      http://www.omegahat.org

D.

messages.subject: [S] discriminant analysis; large and high-dim datasets with MCLUST
messages.subject_clean: [S] discriminant analysis; large and high-dim datasets with MCLUST
messages.body_plain:
Issues :

   1. discriminant analysis (supervised classification) with MCLUST
   2. MCLUST applied to large data sets
   3. MCLUST applied to high-dimensional data

This posting addresses several recent inquiries concerning the use of MCLUST 
for large or high-dimensional data sets. The MCLUST documentation (README
and technical report) has been updated to reflect these issues.

------------------------------------------
Discriminant analysis and large data sets
------------------------------------------

First, it should be noted that the function estep() in MCLUST can be used
for discriminant analysis (supervised classification). It accepts as input 
the parameters of a Gaussian mixture (means, covariances, and mixing 
proportions) and a model specification,  and returns conditional
probabilities which can be converted to a classification if desired.

Large data sets can be classified by first clustering a subset of the data, 
and then classifying the remaining observations by discriminant analysis 
(as was done e.g. with the MRI brain scan image in Banfield and Raftery,
Biometrics 49, 1993). Within MCLUST, the function emclust() can be run 
on a subset of the data to find the clusters, and the optimal conditional 
probabilities obtained via summary(). The function mstep() can then be
invoked to give the associated maximum likelihood parameters. New observations
are then classified using estep() with these parameters as input.

emclust() and emclust1() also include a provision for using a subsample of
size k of the data in the hierarchical clustering phase before applying EM
to the full data set. This strategy is often adequate for data sets that
are large but not extremely large in size.

---------------------
High dimensional data
---------------------

Models in which the orientation is allowed to vary between clusters (EEV, VEV,
and VVV in the current version of MCLUST) have O(d^2) parameters per cluster,
where d is the dimension of the data. For this reason, MCLUST may not work 
well or may otherwise be inefficient for these models when applied to 
high-dimensional data. It may still be possible to analyze such data with
MCLUST by restriction to models with fewer parameters (the spherical models EI
and VI and the constant variance model EEE in MCLUST), or else by applying a
dimension-reduction technique such as principal components. 

Note that none of the methods currently in MCLUST can handle datasets in which
the number of observations is smaller than the data dimension.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Default settings for trellis
messages.body_plain:
Well, it seems that I am not the only one who has had to resort to
modifying the trellis code to give more flexibility in the way defaults
are handled. Many thanks to the follwing respondants:

"Patrick Connolly" <P.Connolly at hort.cri.nz>
John Maindonald <john.maindonald at anu.edu.au>
"Gunter, Bert" <bert_gunter at merck.com>
John Wallace <jrw at fish.washington.edu>

My original questions were how to use the defaults to set the folloing
behaviors withouth having to do it on the command line for every trellis
command:

 1) increase the size of the strip text
 2) get rid of the strip colors
 3) increase the size of the axis and xlab,ylab text

Patrick provided a function very similar to F. Harrell's
trellis.strip.blank (library Hmisc) which sets the strip colors to 0.
This works very well for #2. John Maindonald and Bert Gunter also
provided workarounds using custom strip functions. 

For #1, John Wallace made a change to render.trellis very similar to the
one that I described in my posting. Basically, strip.default indicates
that the default values for par.strip.text are obtained from the
trellis.settings$add.text. However, the render.trellis fcn over-rides
this default. John added his own default "add.strip.text", whereas I
only made it use the existing default "add.text". 

Finally, no one provided a response on how to accomplish #3 using the
defaults. It seems that Statsci hasn't provided a mechanism for setting
the default text size for scale and xlab,ylab without doing it from
within the trellis command. This is a pity, as I will now have to
develop my own defaults mechanism and waste time that I could otherwise
use for more rewarding tasks. 

Once again, thank you for the help.

best regards,
jcd

Original Posting:

"Joseph C. Davis" wrote:

> Hello out there,
> 
> I use Splus trellis graphs for presenting a lot of graphical analysis.
> As they say, "a picture is worth ... ." Anyway, I love the flexibility
> of the formula interface and many other things.

> 2 restrictions:
> 1) have to print to B&W
> 2) put complex graphs on a single page with commentary (ie the graph
> can't take up the whole page)
> 
> These two constraints mean that I need to do the following:
> 1) increase the size of the strip text
> 2) get rid of the strip colors
> 3) increase the size of the axis and xlab,ylab text
> 
> There are mechanisms for controlling these attributes on the command
> line using par.strip.text for (1), trellis.strip.blank from the HMISC
> library for #2,  and a combination of scale=list(cex=X) and
> xlab=list(cex=X) for #3.
> 
> The approaches for #1 and #3, however, require that I type this in
> *every time*. Since there is a defaults database for trellis stettings,
> wouldn't you think that you could set the defaults for these
> characteristics so that the changes stick?
> 
> Theoretically, you can change the setting for "add.text" and it will be
> reflected in the strip headers. However, the render.trellis fcn doesn't

> Although this is easy, one would prefer to merely change the

> this doesn't quite work either. The situation, I believe, is this: In SPlus
> 4.5 for Windows, when you open a graph window with graphsheet() or plot into

> strip.background$col component of these lists also. Once you make the
> changes to BOTH trellis.settings and trellis.settings.colorgrphsht (or
> bwgrphsht), then all your strip backgrounds will come out to whatever
> background you set them to in these lists all the time.

John Wallace wrote:
> 
> I also wanted a good solution for this, so I took a fresh look at it
> (under win9x).
> 
> As Bert was saying there are quite a number of data sets
> 'trellis.settings.*' that can be attached as an attribute to the .Device
> object.  However, they are all attached as 'trellis.settings' on the
> currently active device.  More importantly they can be changed with
> trellis.par.set().
> 
> Note, before I go on, that there is a bug in 'render.trellis' that does
> not allow, is seems, any list to the argument 'par.strip.text' of
> strip.default(), such as the default 'trellis.par.get("add.text")' to ever
> be used. [There is a help page for strip.default()]
> 
> Looking in render.trellis():
> 
> function(..., par.strip.text = list(), ..., strip =strip.default,...)
> 
> ...................
> strip(k, unlist(index[n,  ]), gnames, factor = if(v) NULL else
>   glist[[k]]$levels, shingle = if(v) attr(glist, "endpts")[[k]] else NULL,
>   par.strip.text = par.strip.text)
> .............
> 
> Now 'par.strip.text' is an argument to render.trellis() with a default of
> 'list()'.  So either the default will be used or whatever the user gives
> for 'par.strip.text' in a trellis call [such as to xyplot()].
> 
> Given this bug, I did the following:
> 
> In render.trellis(), changed the default 'list()' of 'par.strip.text' to
> 
>         'trellis.par.get("add.strip.text")'
> 
> 'add.strip.text' is new which I create in:
> 
> trellis.device.bw <- function(..., label.list = list(cex = 1.2, col = 1,
>       font = 1), strip.list = list(cex = 1, col = 1, font = 1))
> {
>         trellis.device(..., color = F)
>         trellis.par.set("strip.background", list(col = rep(0, 7)))
>         trellis.par.set("strip.shingle", list(col = rep(0, 6)))
>         "Use add.text only for xlab and ylab."
>         trellis.par.set("add.text", label.list)
>         "Make a new trellis setting for strip text."
>         trellis.settings$add.strip.text <- strip.list
>         assign("trellis.settings", trellis.settings, frame = 0)
>         invisible()
> 
> Using trellis.settings in this way works, since from the help on
> trellis.settings:
> 
> "If there is no trellis.settings attribute on .Device then the functions
> will use the values in the trellis.settings data set in the Trellis
> library."
> 
> (Of course, the functions find my trellis.settings in frame zero first.)
> 
> Example:
> 
> (Note, the gray from col=3 is probably not what one would want.)
> 
> trellis.device.bw(label.list = list(cex = 2, col = 1, font = 1),
>         strip.list = list(cex = 0.6, col = 3, font = 1))
> 
> states <- data.frame(state.x77,
>                      state.name = dimnames(state.x77)[[1]],
>                      state.region = state.region)
> xyplot(Murder ~ Population | state.region, data = states,
>        groups = as.character(state.name),
>        panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups)
>        text(x, y, groups[subscripts]))
> 
> -------------
> 
> This also helps to get full control for color too:
> 
> trellis.device.color <- function(..., label.list = list(cex = 1.2,
>   col = 1, font = 1), strip.list = list(cex = 1, col = 1, font = 1))
> {
>         trellis.device(..., color = T)
>         "Use add.text only for xlab and ylab."
>         trellis.par.set("add.text", label.list)
>         "Make a new trellis setting for strip text."
>         trellis.settings$add.strip.text <- strip.list
>         assign("trellis.settings", trellis.settings, frame = 0)
>         invisible()
> }
>

probably there is a beautiful package which does this sort of things,

In the meantime, the next function is a very crude option:

draw.ellipse <- function(center,r1,r2,npts=100,...){
  x<-seq(0,2*pi,length=npts)
  lines(center[1]+r1*cos(x),center[2]+r2*sin(x),...)
  invisible()
}

plot(runif(10),runif(10))

messages.body_plain:
Here is another simple version, but more general:

ellipse <-
function(b, C, df, level = 0.95, xlab = "", ylab = "",add=T)
# Plot an ellipse with "covariance matrix C, center b, and P-content
# level according the F(df[1],df[2]) distribution.
{
        d <- sqrt(diag(C))
        df <- c(2, df)
        phase <- acos(C[1, 2]/(d[1] * d[2]))
        angles <- seq( - (PI), PI, len = 51)
        mult <- sqrt(df[1] * qf(level, df[1], df[2]))
        xpts <- b[1] + d[1] * mult * cos(angles)
        ypts <- b[2] + d[2] * mult * cos(angles + phase)
        if(add) lines(xpts, ypts)
        else plot(xpts, ypts, type = "l", xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab)
}

messages.subject: RE: [S] 2 questions
messages.body_plain:
Here's a function to draw an ellipse, with the option to fill it in or just
get the coordinates of the points.

It's an extension of a function of John Wallace I got from S-news some years
ago.

Cheers,
Brad

Brad Biggerstaff, Ph.D.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
National Center for Infectious Diseases
Division of Vector-Borne Infectious Diseases
P.O. Box 2087
Fort Collins, CO  80522-2087   U.S.A.
(970) 221-6473              bkb5 at cdc.gov

===================================================
"ellipse"<-
function(cx, cy, rx, ry, theta = 0, yaxis = T, pointsonly = F, fill = F,
...)
{
# function to plot an ellipse with center (cx,cy)
# and major axis/2 along x equal to rx, 
# major axis/2 along y equal to ry
# and rotated through an angle theta (in radians)
# note that a circle is obtained with rx=ry, 
# in which case theta isn't very helpful either
#
# the parameter yaxis adjusts the size correct in the
# y- or x-axis, as plotting is generally not square
# ...so using par(pty="s") will eliminate the need for this
#
# the parameter pointsonly determines if a plot is
# added-to or the values of the points are returned
# in a list
#
# fill is a flag to indicate filling in the ellipse
#
# ... is useful for arguments to polygon, such as color 
#     and density
#
# this is an adjustment by Brad Biggerstaff 
# on 27 April 1999 to the funtion circle() written
# by John R. Wallace, as noted below
#
# the original function was obtained from S-news
#
# Brad Biggerstaff (bkb5 at cdc.gov)
# May, 1999
#
#   cx, cy, coordinates for centre; r is radius
#   yaxis = T, radius is correct on the y axis
#   yaxis = F, radius is correct on the x axis    
#   DATE WRITTEN:  1994      LAST REVISED:   17 July 1995
#   AUTHOR:  John R. Wallace (jw at u.washington.edu)
#
#
        z <- (0:360 * pi)/180
        pin <- par()$pin
        usr <- par()$usr
        adj <- (pin[2]/pin[1])/((usr[4] - usr[3])/(usr[2] - usr[1]))
        if(yaxis) {
                x <- sin(z) * rx * adj
                y <- cos(z) * ry
        }
        else {
                x <- sin(z) * rx
                y <- (cos(z) * ry * 1)/adj
        }
        xprime <- x * cos(theta) + y * sin(theta) + cx
        yprime <- y * cos(theta) - x * sin(theta) + cy
        if(!pointsonly) {
                if(fill)
                        density <- -1
                else density <- 0
                polygon(xprime, yprime, density = density, ...)
                invisible()
        }
        else list(x = xprime, y = yprime)
}

======================================================

messages.subject: [S] S-Plus Speed and Data Base Size
messages.subject_clean: [S] S-Plus Speed and Data Base Size
messages.body_plain:
This question arises more out of curiosity than any particular
problem.  I'm running S-Plus 4.5 R2 on a 350 MHz Pentium-II NT 4
workstation with 384 MB of memory.  I have a function that performs a
permutation test on density estimates.  When I wrote it, I vaguely recall
that it required about 10 min to execute.  Now it's about 30 min.  The
only thing that's changed since then is the number of objects in my
S-Plus data base, which has risen to over 4000.  This database is the
foundation for my PhD work and so contains a fair number of data sets
that, while I sincerely hope I will not use (because it would mean more
work and delays), I'm not ready to throw out.

        Clearly, the startup is slower, because S-Plus must perform all
the mappings between file names and data set names.  But, is S-Plus's
execution speed significantly affected by the number of objects in the
data base?  I've checked various sources and haven't seen a definitive
answer, but I know that if such an answer exists, one of you will have it!

                Kim Elmore, [N5OP, PP ASMEL/Glider 2232456]

messages.subject: [S] GUI Graphs: Followup
messages.body_plain:
A while ago, I asked if anyone knew how to create plots using the
S-Plus 4.5 GUI to create plots where the sense of an axis is reversed and
labels are correct.

        I want to thank Andreas Krause and Rolf Turner for their answers.
While they didn't have a way to do this from the GUI directly, seeing
whatthey did helped me to hack the problem.  Here are the solutions they
supplied:

--------------------------
>>From Andreas.Krause at genedata.com Wed May 19 11:25:36 1999
Date: Thu, 06 May 1999 09:07:39 +0200
From: Andreas Krause <Andreas.Krause at genedata.com>
To: Kim Elmore <elmore at nssl.noaa.gov>
Subject: Re: [S] GUI Graphs

Hi,
here is a set of a few commands generating a plot where y is going from max(y) 
to min(y).

x <- 100:200
y <- sqrt(x)
plot(x, max(y)-y, axes=F) # reverse y, omit axes
box()
axis(1)
z<-seq(min(y), max(y), length=10) # generate ticks/labels
z <- pretty(z)
axis(2, at=max(y)-z, z) # reverse z in analogy to y

---------------------------

messages.subject: RE: [S] SPlus - Java Integration
messages.body_plain:
First of all, I'm more of developer and less
of an S expert so please forgive me if I get 
things wrong.

I got a whole load of responses to this question. 
So here is the summary :-

1.Embed a JVM inside S
  This allows Java to be callable from within S.

2.For a remote client to send requests to S 
  over Corba.
  
Check these out at http://www.omegahat.org for 
Java/SPLus integration. I understand, they hope to 
release products within the next few months.

3.On Windows, its possible to use ActiveX automation. 
  We use Unix, so I haven't investigated this
  any further.

4.Have a Java server which execs the S command process.
  A Java client can talk to the Java server using RMI.   
  Providing stdin and stdout are redirected, requests 
  can be piped into the S command process 
  and the output can be captured, parsed and sent back 
  to the client.

5.Wrap the C API in Java/JNI. You have to still code
  up new routines etc etc in S. Its just that the invocation
  method is via Java. 

I decided to continue with option 5. and I now have 
a very basic working Java/JNI library to: 
- open a connection, 
- read in some inputs, perform a hard-wired routine
  and return the output.
- close a connection. 

When I get the time, I hope to further develop this into: 
* a proper management of connections as you would if you've messed 
  with JDBC ;-)
* better handling of generic requests
* turn the library into fully fledged Java RMI server
  providing an analytics service.

messages.subject: Re: [S] quantiles of non-central chisq
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Jim Stapleton for answering my request for a function to
calculate the quantiles of a non-central chi-squared distribution.

The function is as follows:

Date: Wed, 19 May 1999 16:40:50 -0400
From: James Stapleton <stapleton at stt.msu.edu>
To: Ranjan Maitra <maitra at math.umbc.edu>
Subject: Re: [S] quantiles of non-central chisq

> qchisq2
function(p, nu, delta = 0, ep = 0.0001)
{
#This function finds the quantile corresponding to p
#for the noncentral-chisquare distribution with 
# nu degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter delta.
#The functions "newton" and "dnoncentchisq" are called.
        z <- c(p, nu, delta)
        G <- function(x, z)
        pchisq(x, z[2], z[3]) - z[1]
        g <- function(x, z)
        dnoncentchisq(x, z[2], z[3])
        x0 <- nu + delta + qnorm(p) * (2 * nu + 4 * delta)^0.5
        newton(x0, G, g, ep = ep, z = z)[1]
}
> qchisq2(.5,23,4)
[1] 26.24953
> pchisq(26.24953,23,4)
[1] 0.5000002
> newton
function(x0, G, g, ep = 0.001, z = 0, step = 1, iterations = 20)
{
#Given the function G and its derivative g, 
#newton uses the Newton method, beginning at x0, 
#to find a point xp at which G is zero. G and g
#may each depend on a parameter z. The result is the 
# 3-component vector of an approximation x0 of xp, 
# G(x0, z), and the number ("count") of iterations. 
# x0 satisfies  abs(G(x0, z)) < ep.
# To also get  the vectors of consecutive values of
# x0 and G(x0, z), replace the last line by 
# list(x0, x0vec, Gvaluevec, count).
        x0vec <- x0
        count <- 0
        Gvaluevec <- Gvalue <- G(x0, z)
        while(abs(Gvalue) > ep) {
                r <- Gvalue/g(x0, z)
                d <- min(abs(r), step) * sign(r)
                x0 <- x0 - d
                Gvalue <- G(x0, z)
                Gvaluevec <- c(Gvaluevec, Gvalue)
                x0vec <- c(x0vec, x0)
                count <- count + 1
                if(count > iterations)
                        stop(paste("count >", as.character(iterations)))
        }
#list(x0, x0vec, Gvaluevec, count)
        c(x0, Gvalue, count)
}
> dnoncentchisq
function(x, nu, del)
{
#This function determines the noncentral-chisquare
#density at x for nu degrees of freedom, noncentrality
#parameter del. x may be a vector. The result is the
#density of the noncentral chisquare distribution with
#parameters nu and del, at x.
        if(del == 0) del <- 0.00001
        upper <- floor(del/2 + 5 * (del/2)^0.5)
        kv <- 0:upper
        n <- length(x)
        poiv <- dpois(kv, del/2)
        fv <- matrix(rep(0, n * (1 + upper)), n)
        for(k in 0:upper)
                fv[, 1 + k] <- dchisq(x, 2 * k + nu)
        c(fv %*% poiv)
}
> 

>Dear all,

>Does anyone know of a quick way to obtain the quantiles of a non-central 
>chi-square distribution?

Following my question yesterday regarding how to access the
variance-covariance matrix and sums of squares terms of a regression object,

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY Combining matrices question
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to the many people (Chuck Berry, Andreas Krause, Jean Adams,
Mike Ernst, Mark Smith, Bert Gunter, Tim Hesterberg,Phil Spector)
who responded to my question:

> I have N matrices of dimension (pxq) that are called
> fit.1, fit.2, fit.3, ... , fit.N.  I would like to "stack" 
> the second column from each matrix so that I end up with
> one matrix of dimension (pxN) x 1. 

There were many solutions that work, some are posted
below.  The first solution stores the data in a 3d array
so that data other than the 2nd column will be available.
Phil Spector's solution protects against memory problems if
N is large.  Thanks to all for the numerous prompt replies!

--------------------------------------------------
>>From Bert Gunter:

  fit.ar<- numeric(p*q*N)
  dim(fit.ar)<- c(p,q,N)
  for(i in 1:N)fit.ar[,,i]<-get(paste("fit",i,sep="."))
  result <- matrix(fit.ar[,2,])
--------------------------------------------------
>>From Jean Adams:

  matrix(sapply(1:N, function(x) 
     eval(parse(text=paste("fit.", x, sep="")))[, 2]), ncol=1)

-------------------------------------------------------
>>From Phil Spector:

Here's something that will work just fine, as long as N
doesn't get too big:

result <- NULL
for (i in 1:N){
    result <- c(result,get(paste("fit.",i,sep=""))[,2])
}

The problem is that if N or nrow(fit.i) is very large, this may hit off
one of Splus' memory leaks.  If so, something like this would probably
be safer:

nr <- nrow(fit.1) # assuming that all the fit.i matrices are the same size
result <- numeric(N * nr)
start <- 1
finish <- nr
for (i in 1:N){
    result[start:finish] <- get(paste("fit.",i,sep=""))[,2]
    start <- start + nr
    finish <- finish + nr
}

This way, you allocate all the memory at once, so it avoids some memory
problems.  But for moderate sized problems, the first solution should be
ok.

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-plussers

My apologies if this question is not sufficiently related to S-Plus.

I have a number of logistic regression models (GAM with smoothing and
family=binomial) predicting the occurrence of different plant species in
grasslands. I have used cross-validation to predict the occurrences in test-data
subsets and have compared the predictions with the observed occurrences.

messages.subject: [S] summary re: profile likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for delay in posting summary re: profile likelihood

Rod Ball suggested I look at profile.glm() 

It is from the MASS library and a breif comment about it was given on 
page 237 of Modern Applied Statistics with S-PLUS. Second Edition 
by W. N. Venables and B.D. Ripley

I initially had some difficulties using it until a colleague reminded me
 to check if my MASS library was current ;-)

Using the MASS library I downloaded today it was quite straightforward to 
extract profile likelihood quanities - the following "rough" code replicates
the 
profile deviance shown on page 264 of McCullagh and Nelder, 
Generalized Linear Models, Second Edition. 

It was however, at least on my current set up, unable to handle unbounded 
profile likelihoods that were the subject of my initial enquiry. For 
completeness I have added a toy example of this kind with the direct use 
of the offset command to plot the profile deviance. 

Also, "dave fournier" <otter at otter-rsch.com>, mentioned that he had stand 
alone software that was very good at non-linear modeling and profile 
likelihood.

 

library(MASS)

glm1<-glm(cbind(c(1,2),c(3,1)) ~ c(0,1),family=binomial)
glm1

prof<-profile(glm1)$"c(0, 1)"

plot(prof[,2][,2],prof[,1]^2)
abline(h = 2.71,v = 1.792)

#example of unbounded profile likelihood
glm1<-glm(cbind(c(0,2),c(3,1)) ~ c(0,1),family=binomial)
glm1

glms<-rep(NA,10)
for(i in 1:10){
glms[i]<-glm(formula = cbind(c(0,2),c(3,1)) ~ offset(c(0,(i -
5)/2)),family=binomial)$deviance

}

plot(((1:10) - 5)/2,glms)

#here profile fails
prof<-profile(glm1)$"c(0, 1)"

messages.subject: [S] Problem w/quadprog.
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to use the QuadProg library to fit a penalized glm with
some inequality restrictions on the parameters. I'm using SPLUS 4.5
for Windows. Here is the core of the code:

                H <- t(X) %*% diag(mu) %*% X * (-1)
                dvec <- apply(sweep(X, 1, y - mu, "*"), 2, sum)
                Dmat <- (-1) * H + 2 * penalty * t(X) %*% K %*% X
                b <- solve.QP(Dmat, dvec, A, b0)$solution
                mu <- as.vector(exp(X %*% b))

This is contained in a loop, naturally. The model is a poisson glm.
For simplicity assume that there is no penalization (i.e., penalty =
0) and we can even effectively remove the inquality constraints by
specifying sufficiently small values in A. Now, When I run this for
some reason the b's diverge so that the mu's become huge to the point
where SPLUS thinks that Dmat is no longer positive definite. If I
replace the fourth line of code above with

                b <- b - solve(H) %*% dvec

then everything works fine as expected. I just can't figure-out why I
cannot solve the same problem via quadratic programming. If anybody
could see a flaw (and a correction!) in my approach I'd be greatful.

Thanks in advance.

Tim

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: Coefficient Constraints in lm
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to all those who responded to my original question (Albyn
Jones, Michael Li, Jean Adams, Andrew Sinclair, John Maindonald,
Berwin Turlach, Nick Ellis, Rolf Turner, Bill Venables, Christian
Keller, Patrick Connolly, and several others who didn't provide names)

The original question was:

> 
> There is probably an easy solution to this problem that I am overlooking,
> but here goes....
> 
> Can I estimate a model using lm where I constrain X1 and X2 to be equal?
> For example:
> 
> mod1<-lm(Y~X1+X2, constrain X1 to equal X2)
> 
> mod2<-lm(Y~X1+X2)
> 
> anova(mod1,mod2)
> 
> Two questions are:
> 1.  What code do I use to estimate mod1?
> 2.  Can I use the anova function to contrast the two models?

Several people correctly pointed out that I wanted to "constrain the X1 and
X2 COEFFICIENTS to be equal", not constrain X1 and X2 to be equal....

Question 1:

As I suspected, the answer was simple, and pretty much the universally
agreed upon solution to question 1 was:

mod1<-lm(Y~I(X1+X2))

An alternative was to create a new variable Z=X1+X2 and use Z as the 
independent variable.

Question 2:

I got some mixed feedback on question 2; however the majority of the
answers stated that the two models were nested, and thus the use of the
anova function in this case was appropriate.

Thanks again,

Paul Bliese
Walter Reed Army Institute of Research
Washington, DC 20307
bliese at wrair-emh1.army.mil

messages.subject: Re: [S] code for growing and pruning trees
messages.subject_clean: [S] code for growing and pruning trees
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 24 May 1999, Gus V. Schmetz wrote:

> Hello S-users,
> 
> Does anyone have the source code to the C functions "grow" and "prune"
> that are used by the S functions tree() and prune.tree() ?

They are part of the AT&T S3 code: only holders of source code licenses
have that code. However, read on.

> If not, I would like to know what algorithms those functions use:
> what is the splitting criteria in "grow" and what is the combining
> criteria in "prune"?

The code for prune.tree is now that of library treefix in the V&R library
bundle: there is not a combining criterion: cost-complexity pruning is
used. The source for treefix is available on statlib (look for MASS2).

The splitting criteria in grow is the reduction in deviance: see the 
Clark & Pregibon paper in the White Book or lots of later writings.
Although I have never seen the code for grow, my Tree library
(at http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/S) works in essentially the same way: it
was actually written from the spec to find some bugs in tree().

You might also be interested in the rpart library on statlib, for which
the source is provided.

--

Change the $(SHOME)/library/S_FLAGS file. That has

CC=gcc

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Random Effects model with a binomial response
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Random Effects model with a binomial response
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone for their responses. I received several requests to
post a summary. Most responses suggested I look at Vinent Carey's
Generalized Estimating Equations functions (gee and yags), available at
http://biosun1.harvard.edu/~carey/index.ssoft.html#geedet, or at the
OSWALD suite of functions at
http://www.maths.lancs.ac.uk/Software/Oswald. Respondents also pointed
out (i) that Oswald has an outdated version of the gee function, and
(ii) that gee and yags are not true random effects models. 

Detailed responses follow:

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Jose Pinheiro:

> Neither nlme, nor lme were designed to be used with non-normal
> response. You should use a generalized linear mixed-effects models
> for such cases. An excellent software that handles this type of
> model is OSWALD, whose homepage is found at the address
>
>      http://www.maths.lancs.ac.uk/Software/Oswald

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Chuck Cleland:

>     You might want to take a look at Vincent Carey's generalized estimating
> equation (GEE) library for this.  For background on the technique, refer to
> papers by Liang, Zeger and probably others.  The library is available at the
> following location:
>
> http://lib.stat.edu/DOS/S/gee.zip

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Renaud Lancelot:

> If you want to stay with S+, you will have to go to GEE models which
> allow one level of grouping. These are marginal models, i.e. they just
> take into account the cluster effect to provide adjusted population
> means and standard errors. You can specify different correlation
> structures (probably a compound symmetry in your case) as well as
> different glm families and link functions. There are (at least) two
> available software by the same author, Vincent Carey
> (http://biosun1.harvard.edu/~carey/index.ssoft.html#geedet): gee() and
> yags().

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Brian Ripley:

> > Is it possible to use nlme() for a similar model with a binomial
> > response? I can't quite see how to code it from the documentation.
> 
> Yes, it is, but there are bugs in nlme2.1 that made this rather tricky to
> achieve. I would start from nlme3 (available at nlme.stat.wisc.edu/Beta).
> Then what you have to do is to set up a logistic (or whatever) response and
> a variance function allowing the variance to vary with the mean. We found
> it necessary to have a variance function of the form n(0.1 + mu(1-mu)) to
> avoid vary slow convergence when the fitted mu was near one.

> I thought of mentioning [Oswald, gee and yags] but they are not random 
> effects models in
> the usually accepted sense. Certainly gee and yags are not: they are models
> for correlated binomial responses, not for binomial responses with random
> effects.  Oswald may have changed, but last time I looked at it it was
> based on an old version of Carey's work. (As the version on that page is
> nearly a year old, it looks the same: a buggy version of Carey's ALR and
> GEE).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Viswanath Devanarayan:

> GEE is not good enough for your data since you have random effects
> (if it's just a repeated measures problem with no other random effect, then 
> GEE is 
> fine).If you are familiar with SAS, you could try the GLIMMIX macro available 
> at the SAS
> web-site.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- 
Kieran Healy              email: kjhealy at princeton.edu 
Department of Sociology   
Princeton University      
Princeton, NJ 08544-1010

messages.subject: [S] Wishful thinking (translation scripts)
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I am preparing to leave the protected halls of academe to open a private
consulting practice.  In preparation, one of the things that I did was
check with SAS Institute to find out what a private license costs --
somwhere in the area of $8000+ for the first year and $3-4000 each year
thereafter.  I've been using SAS for 20+ years and generally love it, but
not THAT much.

Now, given that I'm too cheap to pay their exorbitant annual license fees,
I find myself in the position of having to port mountains of SAS code to
S-Plus.  Is anyone aware of any software packages, scripts, etc. that can
help in this somewhat daunting task?

Thanks,

Fred

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Random Effects model with a binomial response (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
Correction:

I had in mind NLMIXED, not NLINMIX. 

NLMIXED is an experimental procedure in SAS 7.0, which directly maximizes
an approximated integrated likelihood using Gaussian quadrature. One of
the examples is for instance probit-normal model with binomial data.

In contrast NLINMIX is a SAS macro developed earlier by SAS Technical
Support (initial coding 1992). Estimation method is similar to that used
in nlme AND is different from the method used in NLMIXED. 

Although NLINMIX can also be used for random effects model
with a binomial response another SAS macro, GLIMMIX (mentioned in your
summary), is more convenient to use. 

Thanks

Andrzej

messages.subject: [S] Drop-out in repeated measures data
messages.body_plain:
Dear S users,

I have repeated measures behaviour data from an experiment on animals
in which for some treatment groups subjects may die part way through
the monitoring period.

If I use something like lme() to model the data and test for treatment
differences in the response, I'm essentially assuming that any missing
observation for a given animal is missing at random.  Clearly this is
unreasonable since an animal's death will depend on its behaviour leading
up to death which in turn depends on the treatment.

The only function I'm aware of in S-Plus which attempts to model such
non-random drop-out is Oswald's pcmid() function.  However, as pointed
out in the Oswald manual, it is very difficult to get convergence with this
function, and I've yet to successfully achieve this. (Actually, I get it telling
me it's converged, and then refit with slightly different starting values and
it converges to something else.  Also the likelihood of the drop-out model
can be less than that of the model without drop-out, which mystifies me.)

Anyway, I was wondering if there are alternative methods available in
S-Plus for correctly analysing this type of data.  I'm using S-Plus 4.5 for
Windows 95.

cheers

Ray Webster
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] perplexing apply() behaviour
messages.body_plain:
I have a matrix where each row contains drugs, as character values, in no
particular order, and their corresponding mic values which are located in
the column next to the drug.  I need to extract the mic for each drug in
turn.  I wrote a function using a  for() loop which works fine but is slow.
I rewrote it using apply().  For any one row, it returns the correct value.
For some combinations of rows it returns the correct values for all.  For
other combinations, some values get killed.  E.g.:

> getmic3(tdat[71:72,],"AMI")
 189 193
   8  32
> getmic3(tdat[70:72,],"AMI")
 187 189 193
   8   8  NA
> getmic3(tdat[72:73,],"AMI")
 193 194
  32  32
> getmic3(tdat[72:74,],"AMI")
 193 194 196
  32  32  NA
> getmic3(tdat[72:80,],"AMI")
 193 194 196 197 198 199 201 202 203
  NA  NA  NA  NA  NA  NA  32  NA  NA

Details:  the data is a mixture of character and numeric values.  It was
imported from Excel, and some of the columns which should be all numeric
come across as character for no reason I can see.  An early version of the
function inside the apply() failed by returning a list rather than a number;
I extracted part of the list and bashed it with as.numeric(), which yielded
the version which works as above.  If it helps, the functions are as
follows:

> pullout
function(vec, drug)
{
 as.numeric((vec[as.numeric(which(vec == drug | vec == paste("",
  drug)) + 1)])[[1]])
}

> getmic3
function(data, drg1)
{
 assign("drg", drg1, frame = 1)
 out <- apply(data, 1, pullout, drg)
 out
}

I'd appreciate any suggestions as to how apply() is using one row to corrupt
another.

    Peter Wollan
    wollan at mayo.edu

c

messages.subject: [S] make Win4.5 resemble Win3.3
messages.body_plain:
S-Plus Users:

   In a final attempt to give up S-Plus for Windows 3.3 and rely only on S-Plus
for Windows 4.5 r2, I am trying to make 4.5 r2 look more like Win 3.3.  What I
basically want is to startup with only a command line interface and no toolbars
of any kind.  I have figured out the first part.

guiSetOption("StartupCommandLine", "T")
guiSetOption("StartupObjectBrowser", "F")

   For the second part, hiding all toolbars, I tried adding the following lines
to the end of my .First() function.

.First <- function(){
        #
        #other housekeeping#
        # 
        guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "Standard", Hide = T)
        guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "CommandWindow", Hide = T)
}

   This does not seem to work from session to session.  In other words, within a
session these lines have the desired effect, but the toolbars return at the
start of the next session even with these lines as part of .First(). 
Surprisingly (to me), if the first call I make at the start of a session is
(another) to .First(), the toolbars *are* removed.  So, I am looking for a way
to get rid of these command line toolbars which I won't have to do at the
beginning of every session.

thanks,

Chuck Cleland

> From: Chuck Cleland <clelancm at UMDNJ.EDU>

S-Plus
> for Windows 4.5 r2, I am trying to make 4.5 r2 look more like Win 3.3.  What I
> basically want is to startup with only a command line interface and no 
toolbars
> of any kind.  I have figured out the first part.
> 
> guiSetOption("StartupCommandLine", "T")
> guiSetOption("StartupObjectBrowser", "F")

Or set them from the menus: they persist for the current working directory.

>    For the second part, hiding all toolbars, I tried adding the following 
lines
> to the end of my .First() function.
> 
> .First <- function(){
>       #
>       #other housekeeping#
>       # 
>       guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "Standard", Hide = T)
>       guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "CommandWindow", Hide = T)
> }

You need to put GUI things in .guiFirst(), not .First(). The former runs
later in the start-up sequence. (Not tested for your example.)

If you really only want a command-line interface, consider using 
SHOME\cmd\Sqpe, which starts up fast and gives access to everything
you had in 3.3 excepting on-screen graphics. I think in that version
you need to set SHOME, something like

set SHOME=c:/S/splus45
set S_WORK=c:/S/splus45/users/ripley  # or have a _Data in this directory.
c:\S\splus45\cmd\sqpe

   What I basically want is to startup with only a command line interface and no
toolbars of any kind.

   Many thanks to Brian Ripley, Frank Harrell, and Brad Biggerstaff.  The
guiModify() calls need to be put into .guiFirst().  This worked.  Respondents
also noted that one can use sqpe.exe at the DOS prompt for a basic, no-frills
command line interface.  To use sqpe.exe, make sure to set the SHOME environment
variable and a S_WORK directory.  On my machine, I created the following folder

c:\progra~1\splus45\cmd\_Data

and added the following line to my autoexec.bat file

SET SHOME=c:/progra~1/splus45

   These changes allowed me to launch sqpe.exe from the c:\progra~1\splus45\cmd
directory with success.

Thanks again, 

Chuck Cleland

messages.subject: [S] Summary: get(objectname) but not here
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to many useful replies to the issue of using get(objname) from within a 
function
and ignoring local objects of the same name as objname.  Many users suggested 
using
get(objname, where=1), but I did not want to assume that the object was in 
search position
one.  I wanted to use the usual procedure of looking down the search list until 
the object
is encountered, even including the session frame (first).

Chuck Berry came up with the following:

   get(x,where=find(x))

   seems to do the trick. 

   Below I first stumble over 'y' created in the function using get(x), then 
pick 
   up the first 'y' in the search list using get(x,where=find(x)).

   > find("y")
   [1] ".Data"
   > (function(x) {y <- 1;print(find(x));print(summary(get(x)))})("y")
   [1] ".Data"
   Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
       1       1      1    1       1    1 
NULL
   > (function(x) {y <- 1; 
   print(find(x));print(summary(get(x,where=find(x))))})("y")
   [1] ".Data"
   Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu.  Max. 
    0       0      1 1.183   1.007 14.68
   NULL
   > summary(y)
   Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu.  Max. 
    0       0      1 1.183   1.007 14.68
   > 

Tim Hesterberg of MathSoft provided:

   (1) There is a "where" argument to get(); but to use that you need to
   determine just which database it the object is defined on.  See find().

   (2) If the object was defined in the frame of a function that called
   this one, then use the "frame" argument to get().  You need
   to know which frame it is defined on.

   (3) Another possibility is to use eval(), e.g.
   eval(the expression involving get, local=1)
   to evaluate the get expression from frame 1, the expression frame; so 
   this gives the same results as getting the object from outside
   any function.  You could use the frame number for another function,
   e.g. 
   eval(the expression involving get, local=sys.parent(1))
   to evaluate in the calling function's frame; this finds the object
   either there, or in a permanent database.

   foo _ function(objectname){
     h _ 3
     y _ eval(call("get", objectname), local=1)
     y
   }

   h _ 7
   foo("h")

   # y gets 7

Charles Roosen of MathSoft gave:

   I think you can do something like

   eval(as.name(objectname), sys.parent())

Bill Dunlap of Mathsoft sent:

   You could do
   eval(as.name("name"), local=F)
   to get it from any database  (or frame 1) but not the local frame.
   You really want local=nframe where nframe is the frame from which
   a function was originally called with name as an argument.

I like the eval() solutions best.  Here is a test:

f <- function(w) {
  x <- 0
  eval(as.name(w), local=F)
}

assign('x', 3, frame=0)  # in session frame
find(x)
character(0)

f('x')
[1] 3

x <- 33   # in search pos. 1
find(x)
_Data
f('x')
[1] 3

Note that x is still covered up by x in session frame, as it should be.

j <- 44   # in search pos. 1
find(j)
_Data

f('j')
[1] 44

Thanks again for all the help.  I'm impressed to get so many solutions, 
including
3 from MathSoft.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Director, Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Dept of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

Paul Y. Peng wrote:
> It doesn't seem to work either. This is my .guiFirst
> 
> function()
> {
>     guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "Standard", Hide = T)
>     guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "CommandWindow", Hide = T)
>     guiModify("Toolbar", Name = "Graph", Hide = T)

  Paul

  Try changing the .guiFirst as follows:

.guiFirst <- function() {
     guiRemove("Toolbar", Name = "Standard")
     guiRemove("Toolbar", Name = "CommandWindow")
     guiRemove("Toolbar", Name = "Graph")
 }

  I think this should allow one to open graphsheets and move back and forth
between windows without the toolbars reappearing.  To get the toolbars back for
another session, just comment out or remove these lines in .guiFirst.  This is
still not exactly what I had hoped for since there is some dead space between
the top pull-down menu and the command window itself.  But, this is fairly easy
to get rid of (e.g., open a graphsheet), and at least the toolbars seem to be
removed for the life of the session.  Hope this helps others.

Chuck Cleland

messages.subject: [S] ratfor
messages.body_plain:
In olden times people, even quite reasonable people, spoke ratfor and
machines understood them.  Now ratfor seems to be an endangered language,
see http://www.helsinki.fi/~tasalmin/europe_report.html for a nice
survey of other endangered languages. 

As an early native speaker of ratfor, I would like to do my bit to keep
it alive, but my determination to do so has been severely tested over
the last couple of days.  I've been trying to port Rolf Turner's excellent
Delaunay package for S to a linux box that I've recently acquired, and after
considerable frustration have discovered that my version of ratfor
was mistranslating certain switch() statements, yielding a rather well
concealed bug.  Subsequent attempts to use other versions of ratfor
available on the web including ratfor77 from SEP at Stanford, have
produced other, as yet untraced problems.  However, if I simply take
Rolf's ratfor, translate it into fortran(66) on my Solaris machine,
then compile it using g77 on the linux box -- all is well.  

So this brings me to my question.  Does anyone happen to know of a 
reliable version of ratfor in the public domain.  Obviously, I would
like to get my hands on the source used for the Sun version, but
I don't know how to do this.  Any suggestions welcome, well, perhaps not
"isn't about time to learn C?"

messages.subject: [S] Summary: perplexing apply() behavior
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Rod Tjoelker and Patrick Connolly, who suggested ways to solve my
problem without using apply().  I needed to match a character value ("drug")
somewhere in a row of a data frame, and then extract the adjacent numeric
value (mic).  Both solutions suggested separating the characters and the
numbers into separate objects, either a matrix or a vector, and then use
subscripting to extract the values:
either mic.matrix[drug.matrix=="drug"] or mic.vector[drug.vector=="drug"].
Both approaches yield a vector;  the only disadvantage is that the original
row structure is lost, but that can be overcome with a little additional
effort.  Actually, Connolly suggested attaching the drug character values as
names to the numeric vector, but apparently Splus 3.x handled non-unique
names differently than version 4.5 does -- subsetting by name only gives me
the first occurrence of the name, not all occurrences.

Nobody commented on the strange behavior of apply().  After further playing
around, I conclude that apply() can't be used on data frames with mixed
character and numeric columns.   What seems to happen is that sometimes the
function returns a list instead of a number, even though it shouldn't.
Since the error depends on the data, and generates no error message, I
consider it a bug.  It may be related to the routine which imports data from
Excel, which has its own strange behavior.  (that applies to both Excel and
the import routine).

    Peter Wollan
    wollan at mayo.edu

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 28 May 1999, Laurie Becker wrote:

> 
> Hello,
> 
> I have run into a problem with predict.gam and hope that someone can shed
> some light on this.  Earlier this month a similar error message was posted
> to the list but I haven't seen a solution posted.  My models consist of
> factors and continuous data, some with "lo()" terms.  I have checked to make
> sure that none of the values in my newdata set are more extreme that those
> in the original.  I have also made sure that all the levels in my factors
> are present in both data sets. One of my four models can be run w/
> predict.gam and based on the variables in each I have tracked the possible
> problem down to four variables that each have lo() terms.  Beyond looking
> for extreme values, I am not certain how next to proceed.  I am working with
> SPlus 4.0 on an NT.
> 
> ERROR MESSAGE:
> 
> > ht4pred1 <- predict.gam(ht4gam5xy, valid.22, type = "response",se.fit = F)
> Warning messages:
> Warning in safe.predict.gam(object, newdata, type, se.fit, terms): There is
> a 2.218% discrepancy between the original and the re-fit used to achieve
> 'safe' predictions
> Warning messages:Warning in .Fortran("lowese",: eval ü©ñÒMbP¿j¼t"ð?
> 0.20125
> Warning messages:Warning in .Fortran("lowese",: upperlimit lowerlimit eval
> ü©ñÒMbP¿j¼t"ð? 0.19771
> Error in .Fortran("lowese",: extrapolation not allowed with blending
> Dumped

This is telling you that lo thinks you are extrapolating one of the lo
terms. I assume they are terms in one variable: with terms in two it
is multivariate extrapolation that counts. However, lo works by
saving a discretized representation, and what it really means is that you
are extrapolating on that representation. By rounding error, I think it
can get this wrong: the same extreme value as in the fit can be
regarded as extrapolation.

Nothing can be done about this, BUT are you sure that a gam with four
lo terms makes any sense at all?  For example, such fits usually have
multiple maxima in the likelihood, and gam makes no attempt to find them.
Almost all the examples I have seen with only two smooth terms have
co-curvity problems, usually undetected ones. (There are some nice
examples in Bowman & Azzalini's book.)  I would regard neural nets (say) as
a much safer bet for prediction (and they will extrapolate, mildly).

--

Try reading the help page:

DESCRIPTION:
       Returns a vector or array by applying a specified function
       to sections of an array.

A data frame is not an array, and it is coerced to one.
Arrays are of one type.  So what you are attempting is not documented
to work: don't blame your tools for not being what you wish them to be.

I found, that the "aov" of the menu (Splu4.5 windows) can provide the

are assuming a balance design, something like
an even number of observations in all the levels for the fixed factor
that you are interested.   SAS proc MIXED include an
option that takes into account "unbalanced" data (which is the most
common situation), and estimate the LSMeans using a
weight factor related to the number of observations per level.    Have
anybody in the SPLUS galaxy work around estimating
LSMeans for unbalanced data ? or any suggestion how to estimate them....

(by the way, the aov Menu also provides the Type III fixed factors test,
something that should be standard for GLM and GAMs,)

Still learning, ....

Mauricio Ortiz

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 28 May 1999, Mauricio Ortiz wrote:

> 
> Hi
> 
> I found, that the "aov" of the menu (Splu4.5 windows) can provide the
> "adjusted" or LSmeans for a GLM fixed factors,
> there are similar to the SAS proc GLM  lsmeans, however, these LSmeans
> are assuming a balance design, something like
> an even number of observations in all the levels for the fixed factor
> that you are interested.   SAS proc MIXED include an
> option that takes into account "unbalanced" data (which is the most
> common situation), and estimate the LSMeans using a
> weight factor related to the number of observations per level.    Have
> anybody in the SPLUS galaxy work around estimating
> LSMeans for unbalanced data ? or any suggestion how to estimate them....
> 
> (by the way, the aov Menu also provides the Type III fixed factors test,
> something that should be standard for GLM and GAMs,)

The `aov Menu' invokes model.tables, and you should look at its help page
for its restrictions.

Some of us feel that type III sum of squares and so-called ls-means are
statistical nonsense which should have been left in SAS. As you are not
in the SAS world here, be aware that the G in glm and gam is `generalized'
not `general' (SAS's GLM merely highlights that for many years it was
incapable of fitting a linear model with factors and continuous variables).
There are no `Type III fixed factors test's for glms and gams to my
knowledge.

Look back at past discussion here, and especially Bill Venables' `Exegesis'
paper which you can find on-line at

ftp://ftp.statsci.com/pub/yonnie/Venables.pdf

which says:

`I was profoundly disappointed when I saw that S-PLUS 4.5 now provides Type
III sums of squares as a routine option for the summary method for aov
objects. I note that it is not yet available for multistratum models,
although this has all the hallmarks of an oversight (that is, a bug) rather
than common sense seeing the light of day. When the decision was being
taken of whether to include this feature, because the FDA requires it a few
of my colleagues and I were consulted and our reply was unhesitatingly a
clear and unequivocal No, but it seems the FDA and SAS speak louder and we
were clearly outvoted. ...'

After reading that article, perhaps you can tell us why you know better
than Bill what `should be standard' in S-PLUS?

Brian Ripley

messages.subject_clean: [S] Least Square Means in Splus found it BUT ...
messages.body_plain:
> "When the decision was being taken of whether to include this feature, 
>  because the FDA requires it..."
  
I have worked as a statistician in FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and
Research (CDER) for 12 years, and agree that the Type III analysis
(estimates) is not the analysis of choice in almost all situations (I
confess I did argue for Type III analyses in my youth.).  For insight
into this, Dr. Venables' `Exegesis' paper is well worth reading and
understanding.  

Can anyone tell me what part of FDA requires a Type III analysis?  I am
not aware of any document that says CDER requires a "Type III" analysis.
 It is possible that one or more of the 80 CDER statisticians asks for
Type III sums of squares, but I have spent a far amount of time
explaining to my FDA/CDER colleagues that the notion that "Type III is
Truth" is nonsense.  Can anyone provide a name (anonymously, if you
like) of the person/document that says FDA requires it?  Or is that one
or more of CFSAN, CBER, CVM, CDRH etc. requires them?  I would like to
get this sorted out within FDA.

BTW, I will have a poster session on this topic at the ASA meetings in
Baltimore (session 105, #28) for anyone interested in more detailed
discussions of this as it relates to stratified clinical trials.

Jay

> analysis.  It is possible that one or more of the 80 CDER
> statisticians asks for Type III sums of squares, but I have spent a
> far amount of time explaining to my FDA/CDER colleagues that the
> notion that "Type III is Truth" is nonsense.  Can anyone provide a
> name (anonymously, if you like) of the person/document that says FDA
> requires it?  Or is that one or more of CFSAN, CBER, CVM, CDRH
> etc. requires them?  I would like to get this sorted out within FDA.

My understanding from the earlier discussion was that there was a
perception, whether well-founded or not, that the FDA requires (maybe
only sometimes) Type III sums of squares.  It would be a service to
enlightened statistical analysis to extract from the FDA an official
assurance that they do not require Type III sums of squares.

Interactions build on main effects.  Second order interactions build
on third order interactions.  We get parimonious descriptions by not
including any higher order of interaction than we can justify.  Forms
of analysis which ignore this hierarchy of terms lead to mathematics
which some may find interesting.  Presumably this is how they entered
SAS.  For model-building they are at odds with the principle of
parsimony, and severely complicate already difficult issues of model
selection and hypothesis testing.  I hope Bill's paper will be widely
read.

# TO: mzhang at cshl.org

# > Hi,
# > Is there any Splus/S implementation of Kohonen Self-organizing Map?
# > Michael

# Hello Michael,

# Some years ago I wrote a SPLUS program to solve the
# travelling salesman problem by the algorithms found in
# H. Ritter, T. Martinetz, K. Schulten (1990): Neuronale Netze,
# Addison-Wesley. The algorithm uses Kohonen's Self-organizing Map.
# The function was only used for demonstration.
# I am sorry that there is no further documention of the program
# but perhaps it may help you.
#
# Peter Wolf
# pwolf at wiwi.uni.bielefeld.de

# maxloop <--> number of iterations
# anzorte <--> number of places/cities

"TSP"<-
function(maxloop = 10, anzorte = 10)
{
        orte <- runif(2 * anzorte)
        orte <- orte/max(orte)
        orte <- matrix(orte, anzorte, 2)
        anzorte <- dim(orte)[1] # initialization
        anz.neu <- 100
        eps <- 0.80000000000000004
        r <- 1:anz.neu
        ek <- ((2 * pi) * r)/anz.neu
        gew <- gewold <- 0.5 + 0.25 * cbind(sin(ek), cos(ek))
        plot(matrix(c(0, 0, 1, 1), 2, 2, T))
        lines(gew)
        points(orte[, 1], orte[, 2])
        rortnr <- 1 + floor(runif(maxloop, min = 0, max = anzorte))
        for(i in 1:maxloop) {
                print(i)        # choose a point
                v <- rortnr[i]  # compute center
                v.mat <- matrix(orte[v,  ], anz.neu, 2, byrow = T)
                d <- gew - v.mat
                abstand.q <- apply(d * d, 1, "sum")
                rstrich <- order(abstand.q)[1]
        #   rstrich.mat<-matrix(gew[rstrich,],anz.neu,2,byrow=T)
# adaption
                sigma.q <- (50 * 0.02^(i/maxloop))^2
                dum <- abs(r - rstrich)
                dum <- matrix(c(anz.neu - dum, dum), anz.neu, 2)
                hrr.str <- exp((-0.5 * apply(dum, 1, "min")^2)/sigma.q)
                gew <- gew + eps * (v.mat - gew) * cbind(hrr.str, hrr.str)
        #   if(0==i%%10){
                par(col = 0)
                lines(gewold)
        #   }
#   if(0==i%%10){
                par(col = 1)
                lines(gew[, 1], gew[, 2])
                gewold <- gew
#   }
        }
        points(orte[, 1], orte[, 2], pch = 1)
        points(gew[, 1], gew[, 2], pch = 1)
}

messages.subject: [S] "the FDA requires..."
messages.body_plain:
I have run into the following in the past, when dealing with a pharm-
acuetical.
     An NDA (new drug application) has succeeded.
     NDAs are a terribly expensive process.  Because of the prior success,
        the next one(s) to go in are made to look as much as possible like 
        the one that worked.  This includes the analysis plan, and probably
        also the tables, layout, font, ...  (I'm reminded of a recent cartoon
        in the paper of a student in front of a terminal, about to start on
        a paper, thinking "Hmmm, I got a B+ with Helvetica once").
     In time, things that worked got labeled as "the FDA requires...".

  In the case in question, some of the correspondence I recieved had a
near priestly tone (humorous in hindsight, a pain in the posterior at the
time).  I followed up people at the FDA, and found no basis for the taboos
that had been invoked.  

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: [S] Type III
messages.body_plain:
The BMDP manual of many years ago had a nice explanation.  Lacking
subscripts, let's assume a 2 way table of the following structure:

        A1      A2      A3      A4
        B1      B2      B3      B4
        C1      C2      C3      C4

  Assume no empty cells, then there are 12 estimable parameters.  The
type III (Yates weighted means) hypothesis is
        rows: .25(a1 + a2 + a3 + a4) = .25(b1+b2+b3+b4) = .25(c1+c2+c3+c4)

That is, the average row effects are identical.  I think this hypothesis makes
sense even without perfect additivity.  (After all, perfect additivity only
exists in simulations: I have real data).  If I know something about the
population of interest, as opposed to the data set, I might argue for
different column weights: public health questions are rational ones.
I also see a lot of similarity between an argument for Yates' test and for
"intention to treat" analyses: some people take their drug, some not, we
know there is differntial treatment effect ('interaction') but still report
the averaged coefficient.

   Now:
    1. Writing this hypothesis in terms of "main effects + interaction"
coefficients is only a recipe for confusion.  It reveals nothing and
obscures much.
        a. First problem: it leads to an algorithm that can be applied
when there are missing cells.  When there are missing cells the contrast
above isn't estimable, and the one the algorithm computes is hogwash.  (A rule
of thumb for SAS-- if type III and type IV are different, both are misguided).
        b. Second problem:  Apostles of the marginality creed think that I'm
doing something odd with iteractions:  several of the S-news responses are  
in that camp.

   2. I have yet to see someone write the hypothesis in the rational way, i.e.,
like above, and then argue that the test makes no sense.  You can argue that
other tests may be better, and they may well be.  (I most often use sequential
sums of squares myself).  Arguments that ___ is the "only" or "best" test
are of course misguided, and like others I cringe at the enthronment of 
type III SS.

    3. To the extent that Splus has copied an algorithm rather than an
idea, we are in for a confusing future.  SAS has lots of good documentation,
but "The four types of estimable functions" is solidly on the negative side of
the ledger.

        Terry T.
